about: MECH0005 is a 15-credit Term 2 module in UCL Mechanical Engineering that builds on the Term 1 introductory module (MECH0003). Its thermodynamics half covers applying the First Law, pure substances and real and perfect gases, the Second Law, reversibility, entropy and introductory gas power, refrigeration and steam cycles. Its fluid mechanics half covers dimensional analysis, control volume and system analysis with the Reynolds Transport Theorem, the continuity, momentum and energy equations, and basic laminar flow. According to the 2026/27 UCL module catalogue it is assessed by an exam (70%) and coursework (30%).
topics: Applying the First Law of thermodynamics
Pure substances, real gases and perfect gases

notes.body:
This module builds on the Term 1 thermofluids material and applies the First Law to a wider range of systems. The key skill is choosing the right system and the right form of the equation.

Sign convention used here: heat supplied to the system is positive and work done by the system is positive. (Some texts use the opposite sign for work; always state yours.)

Forms of the First Law:
- Closed system (control mass): Q − W = ΔU + ΔKE + ΔPE, usually Q − W = ΔU.
- Cycle: ∮δQ = ∮δW, so the net heat in equals the net work out.
- Steady-flow control volume (SFEE): Q̇ − Ẇ = Σṁ_out(h + V²/2 + gz) − Σṁ_in(h + V²/2 + gz).
- Unsteady (transient) control volume: Q − W = (m₂u₂ − m₁u₁)_CV + Σm_out(h + V²/2 + gz)_out − Σm_in(h + V²/2 + gz)_in, integrated over the process, with ΔKE and ΔPE of the contents of the CV usually neglected.

Work in closed systems: boundary work ∫p dV (constant pressure: pΔV; isothermal ideal gas: mRT ln(V₂/V₁); polytropic pVⁿ = constant: (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(n − 1)), plus shaft, electrical and paddle work.

Worked example (polytropic compression): air at 100 kPa occupying 0.1 m³ is compressed to 800 kPa following pV¹·³ = constant.
- V₂ = 0.1 × (100/800)^(1/1.3) ≈ 0.0202 m³.
- W = (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(n − 1) = (100 × 0.1 − 800 × 0.0202)/0.3 ≈ −20.5 kJ. The negative sign means work is done on the gas.

Worked example (filling an evacuated tank): a rigid, insulated, initially evacuated tank is connected to a supply line of air at 300 K and filled. There is no heat or work and nothing leaves, so the transient energy equation gives m₂u₂ = m_in h_line, so u₂ = h_line.
- For an ideal gas with constant specific heats: c_v T₂ = c_p T_line, so T₂ = γT_line = 1.4 × 300 = 420 K.
- The gas ends up hotter than the supply because the flow work done by the line pushing gas into the tank becomes internal energy.

Common device models (steady flow, ΔKE and ΔPE small unless stated):
- Turbine: Ẇ = ṁ(h₁ − h₂), adiabatic.
- Compressor or pump: power input ṁ(h₂ − h₁).
- Nozzle: V₂² = V₁² + 2(h₁ − h₂).
- Throttle: h₂ = h₁.
- Heat exchanger: ṁ_hot(h_in − h_out)_hot = ṁ_cold(h_out − h_in)_cold if externally adiabatic.

Problem-solving routine:
1. Sketch the system and boundary; list what crosses it.
2. State assumptions (steady, adiabatic, ideal gas, negligible KE).
3. Identify the states and fix each with two independent properties; look up or calculate properties.
4. Apply mass and energy balances.
5. Check signs, units and physical sense (for example, an adiabatic turbine cannot produce more work than the enthalpy drop).

Efficiency definitions follow from the First Law: thermal efficiency η = W_net/Q_in for an engine; coefficient of performance COP = Q_L/W_in for a refrigerator and Q_H/W_in for a heat pump.

Exam tips: be explicit about the system type before writing any equation, and do not mix kJ and J when kinetic energy terms appear.

notes.h: Pure substances, real gases and perfect gases
notes.body:
A pure substance has a fixed chemical composition throughout, although it may exist in more than one phase (water as ice, liquid and steam).

Phase-change vocabulary (water at fixed pressure, heated):
- Compressed (subcooled) liquid: below the saturation temperature for that pressure.
- Saturated liquid: about to boil.
- Wet (saturated) mixture: liquid and vapour coexist at the saturation temperature T_sat(p).
- Saturated vapour: the last drop of liquid has just evaporated.
- Superheated vapour: above T_sat for that pressure.
During boiling at constant pressure, temperature stays at T_sat while heat is added.

Property diagrams: on a T–v diagram, the saturation dome joins the saturated liquid and vapour lines, meeting at the critical point (for water about 373.95 °C and 22.06 MPa). Above the critical point there is no distinct boiling. The triple point of water, where solid, liquid and vapour coexist, is at 0.01 °C and about 0.61 kPa.

Dryness fraction (quality): x = m_vapour/m_total in a wet mixture. Mixture properties:
- v = v_f + x(v_g − v_f)
- h = h_f + x h_fg, and similarly for u and s.
The subscripts f and g mean saturated liquid and saturated vapour; fg means the difference g − f.

Worked example (saturated water values from the open-textbook pressure table listed in this pack's sources; other tables differ in the last figure, e.g. h_fg = 2257.5 kJ/kg): at 1 bar (100 kPa), T_sat ≈ 99.6 °C, h_f ≈ 417.5 kJ/kg, h_fg ≈ 2257.4 kJ/kg, v_f ≈ 0.001043 m³/kg and v_g ≈ 1.694 m³/kg.
- Wet steam with x = 0.9: h = 417.5 + 0.9 × 2257.4 ≈ 2449 kJ/kg, and v ≈ 0.001043 + 0.9 × 1.693 ≈ 1.525 m³/kg.
- If v = 1.0 m³/kg at 1 bar, x = (1.0 − 0.001043)/(1.694 − 0.001043) ≈ 0.59.
Values differ slightly between table editions, so quote the source you used.

Using tables: first decide the phase. At a given p, compare T with T_sat (or v with v_f and v_g): v < v_f means compressed liquid (approximate by saturated liquid at the same T); v_f < v < v_g means wet; v > v_g or T > T_sat means superheated, so use the superheat tables, interpolating linearly where needed.

Ideal and perfect gases:
- An ideal gas obeys pv = RT (R = R̄/M), and its u and h depend only on T.
- Many UK texts use 'perfect gas' for an ideal gas whose specific heats are also constant, so Δu = c_vΔT and Δh = c_pΔT exactly. Usage varies between books, so define your terms.
- For air, approximately R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K), c_p = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K), c_v = 0.718 kJ/(kg·K) and γ = 1.4.

Real gases: at high pressure or near saturation, molecules' finite size and attractive forces matter and pv = RT fails. The compressibility factor Z = pv/(RT) measures the departure (Z = 1 for an ideal gas). The ideal gas model is good when the reduced pressure p/p_cr is small or the reduced temperature T/T_cr is high. Steam near saturation should not be treated as an ideal gas; use tables. Equations of state such as van der Waals' add corrections for molecular size and attraction.

Exam tips: always determine the phase before choosing a table, show interpolation steps, and state whether you are treating a gas as ideal or perfect.

The First Law says energy is conserved but not which way processes go. Heat flows spontaneously from hot to cold, not the reverse; work can be converted completely into heat, but heat cannot be converted completely into work in a cycle. The Second Law captures these limits.

Two classical statements:
- Kelvin–Planck: it is impossible for any device operating in a cycle to receive heat from a single reservoir and produce an equal amount of work. Every heat engine must reject some heat to a colder reservoir.
- Clausius: it is impossible for any device operating in a cycle to transfer heat from a colder body to a hotter body with no other effect. A refrigerator needs a work input.
The two statements are equivalent: violating one allows the other to be violated.

Heat engines, refrigerators and heat pumps (magnitudes, with Q_H the heat exchanged with the hot reservoir and Q_L with the cold one):
- Engine thermal efficiency: η = W_net/Q_H = 1 − Q_L/Q_H.
- Refrigerator: COP_R = Q_L/W_in.
- Heat pump: COP_HP = Q_H/W_in = COP_R + 1.

Reversible and irreversible processes: a reversible process can be reversed so that both the system and its surroundings return exactly to their initial states. It is an idealisation, a limit that real processes approach. Sources of irreversibility:
- Friction (mechanical and fluid).
- Heat transfer across a finite temperature difference.
- Unrestrained (free) expansion.
- Mixing of different substances or states.
- Electrical resistance, inelastic deformation, chemical reactions.
An internally reversible process has no irreversibilities within the system; an externally reversible one has none in the surroundings (heat exchanged with reservoirs at the system's temperature).

Carnot principles:
1. No engine operating between two reservoirs can be more efficient than a reversible engine between the same reservoirs.
2. All reversible engines between the same two reservoirs have the same efficiency.
This leads to the thermodynamic temperature scale, Q_H/Q_L = T_H/T_L for reversible cycles, and the Carnot limits (temperatures in kelvin):
- η_Carnot = 1 − T_L/T_H
- COP_R,Carnot = T_L/(T_H − T_L)
- COP_HP,Carnot = T_H/(T_H − T_L)

Worked examples:
- An engine between 800 K and 300 K: η_max = 1 − 300/800 = 0.625. Using Celsius (527 °C and 27 °C) would wrongly give about 0.95.
- A refrigerator between −10 °C (263.15 K) and 25 °C (298.15 K): COP_R,max = 263.15/35 ≈ 7.5; a heat pump between the same temperatures has COP_HP,max ≈ 8.5.
- Checking a claim: an inventor says an engine takes 1000 kJ from a source at 900 K, rejects heat at 300 K and produces 700 kJ of work. The Carnot limit is 1 − 300/900 = 0.667, so at most 667 kJ is possible: the claim violates the Second Law.

Why it matters: to raise efficiency, raise the temperature at which heat is added, lower the temperature at which it is rejected, and reduce irreversibilities.

Exam tips: use kelvin, state which statement or principle you are applying, and when testing a claim compare it with the reversible limit.

Entropy turns the Second Law into a property you can calculate.

Clausius inequality: for any cycle, ∮δQ/T ≤ 0, with equality for a reversible cycle. Because ∮δQ_rev/T = 0, the quantity δQ_rev/T is the change of a property, the entropy S:
dS = δQ_rev/T, with units kJ/K (specific entropy s in kJ/(kg·K)).

Entropy balance for a closed system:
ΔS = ∫δQ/T_boundary + S_gen, with S_gen ≥ 0.
- S_gen = 0 for a reversible process and S_gen > 0 for an irreversible one; S_gen < 0 is impossible.
- For an isolated system, ΔS = S_gen ≥ 0: the increase of entropy principle.
- Entropy can be transferred by heat (and by mass flow in an open system) but it can only be created, never destroyed.

Example (heat transfer across a finite temperature difference): 1000 kJ flows from a reservoir at 500 K to one at 300 K.
- ΔS_hot = −1000/500 = −2.0 kJ/K; ΔS_cold = +1000/300 = +3.33 kJ/K.
- S_gen = 1.33 kJ/K > 0, confirming irreversibility. The larger the temperature difference, the more entropy is generated.

Gibbs (T ds) relations, valid between any equilibrium states:
- T ds = du + p dv
- T ds = dh − v dp

Entropy change of an ideal gas (constant specific heats):
- Δs = c_p ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(p₂/p₁)
- Δs = c_v ln(T₂/T₁) + R ln(v₂/v₁)
For example, isothermal expansion of air to twice its volume: Δs = 0.287 ln 2 ≈ 0.199 kJ/(kg·K).

Incompressible substances (liquids, solids): Δs = c ln(T₂/T₁). Mixing 1 kg of water at 80 °C with 1 kg at 20 °C in an insulated vessel gives 50 °C and ΔS = 4.18[ln(323.15/353.15) + ln(323.15/293.15)] ≈ +0.036 kJ/K, positive as it must be for spontaneous mixing.

Isentropic processes of a perfect gas (reversible and adiabatic, so Δs = 0):
- T₂/T₁ = (p₂/p₁)^((γ−1)/γ) and pv^γ = constant.

Isentropic efficiencies compare real adiabatic devices with the ideal isentropic process between the same pressures:
- Turbine: η_T = (h₁ − h₂)/(h₁ − h₂s) (actual work/isentropic work).
- Compressor: η_C = (h₂s − h₁)/(h₂ − h₁) (isentropic work/actual work).

Worked example: air at 100 kPa and 300 K is compressed adiabatically to 800 kPa with η_C = 0.85.
- T₂s = 300 × 8^(0.2857) ≈ 543.4 K.
- Isentropic work = 1.005 × 243.4 ≈ 244.7 kJ/kg; actual work = 244.7/0.85 ≈ 287.8 kJ/kg.
- Actual T₂ = 300 + 243.4/0.85 ≈ 586.4 K.
- Δs = 1.005 ln(586.4/300) − 0.287 ln 8 ≈ +0.077 kJ/(kg·K) > 0, as expected for an irreversible adiabatic process.

T–s diagrams: the area under a reversible process curve is the heat transferred (∫T ds). Isentropic processes are vertical lines; for cycles, the enclosed area is the net work.

Exam tips: always use kelvin in logarithms and Carnot expressions, check the sign of S_gen, and sketch processes on a T–s diagram.

notes.h: Gas power, refrigeration and steam cycles
notes.body:
Cycles combine the processes studied so far into engines and refrigerators. Idealised cycles show the main trends; real cycles add irreversibilities.

Air-standard assumptions (for internal combustion engines and gas turbines): the working fluid is air, treated as an ideal gas, circulating in a closed loop; combustion is replaced by heat addition and the exhaust by heat rejection; all processes are internally reversible. 'Cold air-standard' analysis also takes specific heats as constant at room-temperature values (γ = 1.4).

Otto cycle (idealised spark-ignition engine): isentropic compression, constant-volume heat addition, isentropic expansion, constant-volume heat rejection.
- η_Otto = 1 − 1/r^(γ−1), where r = V_max/V_min is the compression ratio.
- r = 8: η = 1 − 8^(−0.4) ≈ 0.565. Efficiency rises with r, but knock limits r in petrol engines.

Diesel cycle (idealised compression-ignition engine): heat added at constant pressure, with cut-off ratio r_c = V₃/V₂.
- η_Diesel = 1 − (1/r^(γ−1)) × (r_c^γ − 1)/(γ(r_c − 1)).
- For the same r it is less efficient than Otto, but diesel engines run at much higher r.

Brayton (Joule) cycle (idealised gas turbine): isentropic compression, constant-pressure heat addition, isentropic expansion, constant-pressure heat rejection.
- η_Brayton = 1 − 1/r_p^((γ−1)/γ), with r_p the pressure ratio.
- r_p = 10: η ≈ 0.482.
- The back work ratio (compressor work/turbine work) is large, so component efficiencies matter greatly.

Vapour-compression refrigeration cycle: (1) saturated vapour leaves the evaporator and is compressed to (2) superheated vapour; it condenses to (3) saturated liquid; it is throttled (h₄ = h₃) back to the evaporator pressure; and it evaporates, absorbing heat from the cold space.
- COP_R = (h₁ − h₄)/(h₂ − h₁).
- Example with approximate R-134a table values (0.14 MPa evaporator, 0.8 MPa condenser, isentropic compression): h₁ ≈ 239.2, h₂ ≈ 275.4, h₃ = h₄ ≈ 95.5 kJ/kg, so COP_R ≈ 143.7/36.2 ≈ 3.97. For 0.05 kg/s this gives about 7.2 kW of cooling for 1.8 kW of work.
- A heat pump uses the same cycle with COP_HP = (h₂ − h₃)/(h₂ − h₁).

Rankine cycle (ideal steam power plant): (1) superheated steam expands isentropically in the turbine to (2) wet steam at condenser pressure; it is condensed to (3) saturated liquid; the pump raises it to boiler pressure (4), with w_p ≈ v(p₄ − p₃); and the boiler heats it back to state 1.
- Example (values from IAPWS-95-based steam tables, as printed in Çengel and Boles, Thermodynamics: An Engineering Approach, Tables A-5 and A-6): turbine inlet 4 MPa and 400 °C (h₁ = 3214.5 kJ/kg, s₁ = 6.7714 kJ/(kg·K)); condenser at 10 kPa (h_f = 191.8, h_fg = 2392.1 kJ/kg, s_f = 0.6492, s_fg = 7.4996 kJ/(kg·K)). Older tables give slightly different values (for example h₁ ≈ 3213.6 kJ/kg and s₁ ≈ 6.769 kJ/(kg·K)), which change the answers only in the last figure; use the table your course provides.
- x₂ = (6.7714 − 0.6492)/7.4996 ≈ 0.8163, so h₂ ≈ 191.8 + 0.8163 × 2392.1 ≈ 2144.6 kJ/kg.
- Turbine work ≈ 1069.9 kJ/kg; pump work ≈ 0.00101 × (4000 − 10) ≈ 4.0 kJ/kg; h₄ ≈ 195.8 kJ/kg.
- Heat input ≈ 3214.5 − 195.8 = 3018.7 kJ/kg, so η ≈ (1069.9 − 4.0)/3018.7 ≈ 0.353.
- The pump work is tiny compared with the turbine work, a key advantage of pumping a liquid.

Improving the Rankine cycle: raise boiler pressure and superheat temperature, lower condenser pressure, add reheat (which also keeps turbine exit steam drier) and regenerative feedwater heating. All of these raise the mean temperature of heat addition or lower that of heat rejection, consistent with the Carnot principle.

Exam tips: sketch each cycle on p–v and T–s diagrams with numbered states, state the assumptions, and compare your answer with the Carnot efficiency between the same extreme temperatures as a sanity check.

notes.h: The role of fluid mechanics and dimensional analysis
notes.body:
Fluid mechanics underpins pumps, turbines, pipelines, aircraft, cars, ships, heating and ventilation, blood flow and weather. Many important flows are too complex to solve exactly, so engineers combine conservation laws, experiments and dimensional reasoning.

Dimensional analysis rests on dimensional homogeneity: every term in a valid physical equation has the same dimensions. Base dimensions in mechanics are mass M, length L and time T (plus temperature Θ for heat transfer).
- Velocity: L T⁻¹. Force: M L T⁻². Pressure: M L⁻¹ T⁻². Density: M L⁻³. Dynamic viscosity: M L⁻¹ T⁻¹.

Why use it:
- It reduces the number of variables, so fewer experiments are needed.
- It reveals the groups that control the physics.
- It provides the scaling laws for model testing.

Buckingham Π theorem: if a problem involves n variables containing k independent base dimensions, it can be expressed in terms of n − k independent dimensionless Π groups.
Method (repeating variables):
1. List all relevant variables and their dimensions.
2. Choose k repeating variables that together contain all the base dimensions but do not form a dimensionless group themselves (often ρ, V and a length D).
3. Combine each remaining variable with the repeating variables to make it dimensionless.
4. Express the result as Π₁ = φ(Π₂, Π₃, ...).

Example 1 (drag on a sphere): F depends on ρ, V, D and μ. That is n = 5 and k = 3, so there are 2 groups: F/(ρV²D²) = φ(ρVD/μ). So drag coefficient depends only on Reynolds number, and one curve replaces a large table of experiments.

Example 2 (pendulum): period t depends on length L, g and mass m. With n = 4 and k = 3 there is one group, t√(g/L) = constant. Mass cannot appear, because no other variable contains M to cancel it. Full analysis gives t = 2π√(L/g) for small swings.

Important dimensionless groups:
- Reynolds number Re = ρVL/μ: inertial/viscous forces; governs laminar versus turbulent flow and viscous drag.
- Froude number Fr = V/√(gL): inertia/gravity; free-surface flows, ship waves.
- Mach number Ma = V/c: compressibility; flows above about Ma 0.3 are noticeably compressible.
- Pressure or drag coefficients: Δp/(½ρV²) and F/(½ρV²A).
- Euler number and Weber number (surface tension) appear in other problems.

Similarity and model testing: a model reproduces the full-size flow when it is geometrically similar (same shape, scaled), kinematically similar (velocity ratios the same) and dynamically similar (force ratios the same, i.e. all relevant Π groups equal).
- Example: a 1:4 scale car model tested in air must match Re: ρV_mL_m/μ = ρV_pL_p/μ, so V_m = 4V_p. For a 25 m/s prototype speed, the model needs 100 m/s, which approaches compressible speeds. This shows why full similarity is often impossible and engineers rely on Re-independence at high Re or use a different fluid.
- Matching both Fr and Re at once for ship models is usually impossible with water, so the effects are separated.

Exam tips: tabulate variables with dimensions, state n, k and the number of groups, check each group is dimensionless, and explain the physical meaning of the groups you find.

notes.h: Control volumes and the Reynolds Transport Theorem
notes.body:
Mechanics laws (conservation of mass, Newton's second law, the First Law) are naturally stated for a system: a fixed collection of matter. In fluid mechanics it is usually more convenient to analyse a control volume (CV): a fixed or moving region in space through which fluid flows. The Reynolds Transport Theorem (RTT) links the two.

Definitions:
- B: any extensive property of the fluid (mass m, momentum mV, energy E).
- b = B/m: the corresponding intensive property (1, V, e).
- Control surface (CS): the boundary of the CV; n is the outward unit normal.

RTT for a fixed, non-deforming control volume:
dB_sys/dt = d/dt ∫_CV ρb dV + ∫_CS ρb (V·n) dA
In words: the rate of change of B for the system that occupies the CV at that instant equals the rate of change of B stored inside the CV plus the net rate at which B flows out across the control surface.
- V·n is positive where fluid leaves and negative where it enters.
- For steady flow, the storage term is zero.
- For uniform properties at discrete inlets and outlets, the surface integral becomes Σ(ṁb)_out − Σ(ṁb)_in.

Applying RTT:
- B = m (b = 1): dm_sys/dt = 0 gives the continuity (mass) equation.
- B = mV (b = V): d(mV)_sys/dt = ΣF gives the linear momentum equation.
- B = E (b = e = u + V²/2 + gz): dE_sys/dt = Q̇ − Ẇ gives the energy equation.
So one theorem produces all three control volume equations used in the next topic.

Worked example (unsteady mass balance): a tank of plan area 0.5 m² receives 5 kg/s of water and drains through a pipe of area 0.002 m² at a mean speed of 1.5 m/s.
- Outflow ṁ = ρAV = 1000 × 0.002 × 1.5 = 3 kg/s.
- RTT with b = 1: d(m_CV)/dt = 5 − 3 = 2 kg/s.
- Level rises at dh/dt = 2/(1000 × 0.5) = 0.004 m/s.

Choosing a control volume:
- Cut the control surface perpendicular to the flow where properties are known or wanted (inlets, outlets, jets at atmospheric pressure).
- Include the forces you need to find (cut through bolts or supports if the reaction on a component is required).
- Keep it simple: the CV can be any shape.
- Moving CVs (for example on a moving vane) use the velocity relative to the CV.

System versus CV viewpoints: Lagrangian (follow fluid particles) versus Eulerian (watch fixed points in space). Most engineering measurements and analyses are Eulerian, which is why the RTT is needed.

Exam tips: draw the CV clearly with its inlets and outlets labelled, write the general RTT form before simplifying, and state each assumption (steady, uniform flow at sections, incompressible) as you drop terms.

The three control volume equations follow from the Reynolds Transport Theorem. Together they solve most first-year fluid flow problems.

1. Continuity (conservation of mass):
d/dt ∫_CV ρ dV + ∫_CS ρ(V·n) dA = 0
- Steady flow: Σṁ_in = Σṁ_out, with ṁ = ρAV.
- Incompressible: ΣQ_in = ΣQ_out, so A₁V₁ = A₂V₂.

2. Linear momentum (Newton's second law for a CV):
ΣF = d/dt ∫_CV ρV dV + ∫_CS ρV(V·n) dA
- Steady flow with uniform inlets and outlets: ΣF = Σ(ṁV)_out − Σ(ṁV)_in. This is a vector equation; apply it in each direction separately.
- ΣF includes pressure forces on the control surface (use gauge pressure when the atmosphere acts all round), forces from solid boundaries (often the unknown) and body forces such as weight.

Example (jet on a flat plate): a water jet of diameter 50 mm at 20 m/s strikes a fixed flat plate normally and spreads out sideways.
- ṁ = ρAV = 1000 × 1.963 × 10⁻³ × 20 ≈ 39.3 kg/s.
- In the jet direction the outgoing momentum is zero, so the plate must exert F = ṁV ≈ 785 N on the water, and the water pushes the plate with 785 N.

Example (nozzle on a hose): water flows at 0.01 m³/s through a horizontal nozzle from 80 mm to 30 mm diameter and exits to atmosphere.
- V₁ ≈ 1.99 m/s, V₂ ≈ 14.15 m/s; Bernoulli gives p₁ (gauge) ≈ ½ × 1000 × (14.15² − 1.99²) ≈ 98.1 kPa.
- Momentum on the water: p₁A₁ + F_x = ṁ(V₂ − V₁), so F_x = 10 × 12.16 − 98 091 × 5.027 × 10⁻³ ≈ 121.6 − 493.1 = −371.5 N.
- The nozzle pushes the water upstream with 371.5 N, so the water pushes the nozzle downstream with 371.5 N: the coupling must hold the nozzle on.

3. Energy equation:
Q̇ − Ẇ_shaft = d/dt ∫_CV ρe dV + ∫_CS ρ(h + V²/2 + gz)(V·n) dA
- Steady flow, one inlet and one outlet: this is the SFEE.
- For incompressible flow of a liquid with no heat transfer, the energy equation is written in head form:
p₁/(ρg) + V₁²/(2g) + z₁ + h_pump = p₂/(ρg) + V₂²/(2g) + z₂ + h_turbine + h_L
where h_L is the head loss from friction, which ends up as internal energy (a small temperature rise).
- With no shaft work and no losses, this reduces to Bernoulli's equation. Bernoulli requires steady, incompressible, inviscid flow along a streamline (and no shaft work or heat transfer).

Kinetic energy correction factor: with a non-uniform velocity profile, the true kinetic energy flux is α ṁ V̄²/2, with α = 2 for fully developed laminar pipe flow and close to 1 (about 1.05) for turbulent flow.

Choosing the equation: continuity relates velocities; Bernoulli or the energy equation relates pressures to velocities and heights; momentum gives forces. Many problems need all three.

Exam tips: draw the CV and a force diagram, use gauge pressures consistently, give direction with every force, and remember that the momentum equation still holds where Bernoulli does not (for example across a hydraulic jump or sudden expansion).

In laminar flow, fluid moves in smooth layers with no mixing eddies. Viscous stresses dominate, and many laminar flows can be solved exactly from a force balance with Newton's law of viscosity, τ = μ du/dy.

Laminar or turbulent? In a circular pipe, the Reynolds number Re = ρVD/μ (V the mean velocity) decides:
- Re below about 2000–2300: laminar.
- Higher Re: transitional, then turbulent (the exact value depends on disturbances).
- Example: oil with ρ = 900 kg/m³ and μ = 0.1 Pa·s flowing at 1 m/s in a 20 mm pipe has Re = 900 × 1 × 0.02/0.1 = 180, so it is laminar. Water at the same speed in a 50 mm pipe (μ ≈ 10⁻³ Pa·s) has Re ≈ 50 000, so it is turbulent.

Fully developed laminar pipe flow (Hagen–Poiseuille flow): steady, incompressible, Newtonian flow far from the entrance, where the velocity profile no longer changes along the pipe.
- A force balance on a cylinder of fluid of radius r and length L gives τ = (Δp/L)(r/2): shear stress varies linearly from zero on the axis to a maximum at the wall, τ_w = (Δp/L)(D/4).
- Combining with τ = −μ du/dr and the no-slip condition gives a parabolic profile: u(r) = u_max(1 − r²/R²).
- u_max = 2V (the centreline velocity is twice the mean).
- Volume flow rate: Q = πD⁴Δp/(128μL) (the Hagen–Poiseuille equation). Note the D⁴ dependence: halving the diameter cuts the flow by a factor of 16 for the same pressure drop.
- Equivalently, Δp = 32μLV/D².

Friction factor and head loss: the Darcy–Weisbach equation h_f = f(L/D)(V²/2g) applies to all fully developed pipe flow; for laminar flow f = 64/Re exactly (independent of wall roughness).

Worked example (the oil above, over 10 m of pipe):
- Δp = 32 × 0.1 × 10 × 1/0.02² = 80 kPa.
- Check with Darcy: f = 64/180 ≈ 0.356; h_f = 0.356 × (10/0.02) × 1²/(2 × 9.81) ≈ 9.06 m of oil; ρgh_f ≈ 900 × 9.81 × 9.06 ≈ 80 kPa. The two methods agree.
- Wall shear stress τ_w = Δp D/(4L) = 80 000 × 0.02/40 = 40 Pa.
- Pumping power = QΔp = (π/4 × 0.02² × 1) × 80 000 ≈ 25 W.

Flow between parallel plates:
- Couette flow (one plate moving at speed U, no pressure gradient): linear profile u = Uy/h, uniform shear stress τ = μU/h. This models lubricated bearings.
- Plane Poiseuille flow (both plates fixed, pressure-driven): parabolic profile with u_max = 1.5 V̄.

Entrance length: the profile takes some distance to develop; for laminar pipe flow this is roughly 0.06 Re D (about 0.05–0.06 Re D depending on the definition). For Re = 180 and D = 20 mm, this is about 0.2 m.

Assumptions to remember: Newtonian fluid, incompressible, steady, fully developed, laminar, no-slip at walls. Outside these conditions (turbulence, entrance region, non-Newtonian fluids) the formulas no longer apply.

Exam tips: check Re first, use consistent SI units (μ in Pa·s), and cross-check Δp using both Hagen–Poiseuille and f = 64/Re.

questions.q: A rigid, insulated, evacuated tank is filled with air from a supply line at 300 K. Treating air as a perfect gas with γ = 1.4, what is the final temperature of the air in the tank?
questions.why: With no heat, work or outflow, the energy balance gives u₂ = h_line, so c_vT₂ = c_pT_line and T₂ = γT_line = 420 K: the flow work done by the line heats the gas. 300 K assumes the temperature is unchanged, ignoring the flow work. 214 K divides by γ, which would follow from wrongly writing h₂ = u_line. 311 K applies the factor γ to the Celsius temperature (1.4 × 27 °C ≈ 38 °C ≈ 311 K); the energy balance needs absolute temperature.

questions.q: Air at 100 kPa occupying 0.1 m³ is compressed polytropically (n = 1.3) to 800 kPa, reaching 0.0202 m³. Using the convention that work done by the system is positive, what is the boundary work?
questions.why: W = (p₁V₁ − p₂V₂)/(n − 1) = (10 − 16.16)/0.3 ≈ −20.5 kJ; negative because work is done on the gas. +20.5 kJ has the right size but the wrong sign for compression under this convention. −6.2 kJ omits the division by (n − 1). −16.0 kJ uses the isothermal formula p₁V₁ ln(V₂/V₁) = 10 × ln(0.202), which applies only when n = 1.

questions.q: Steam enters an adiabatic turbine at 4 MPa and 400 °C (h ≈ 3214.5 kJ/kg) with a mass flow of 2 kg/s and leaves at 10 kPa with a dryness fraction of 0.90 (at 10 kPa, h_f = 191.8 and h_fg = 2392.1 kJ/kg; values from IAPWS-95-based tables as in Çengel and Boles). Neglecting kinetic and potential energy changes, find the exit enthalpy and the power output.
markScheme: SFEE with Q̇ = 0, ΔKE, ΔPE ≈ 0: Ẇ = ṁ(h₁ − h₂)
Assumptions stated: steady, adiabatic, negligible KE/PE
Correct sign/interpretation: positive = power output
questions.modelAnswer: For a steady, adiabatic turbine with negligible changes in kinetic and potential energy, the SFEE reduces to Ẇ = ṁ(h₁ − h₂). Exit state: wet steam at 10 kPa with x = 0.90, so h₂ = h_f + x h_fg = 191.8 + 0.90 × 2392.1 ≈ 2344.7 kJ/kg. Power: Ẇ = 2 × (3214.5 − 2344.7) ≈ 1740 kW, about 1.74 MW, positive so it is power output. (An isentropic expansion would reach x ≈ 0.816 and give more work; the higher exit quality here reflects turbine irreversibility.)

questions.q: Wet steam at 1 bar has a dryness fraction of 0.9. Using h_f ≈ 417.5 kJ/kg and h_fg ≈ 2257.4 kJ/kg, what is its specific enthalpy?
questions.why: h = h_f + x h_fg = 417.5 + 0.9 × 2257.4 ≈ 2449 kJ/kg. 2032 kJ/kg is 0.9 × h_fg alone, forgetting to add h_f. 2675 kJ/kg is h_g, the value for dry saturated vapour (x = 1). 643 kJ/kg applies the dryness fraction the wrong way round, h_f + (1 − x)h_fg, which treats x as the liquid fraction.

questions.q: Which statement about real gases is correct?
options: Real gases always have Z greater than 1
A perfect gas has specific heats that vary strongly with temperature
The ideal gas law is accurate for steam close to its saturation line
The compressibility factor Z = pv/(RT) equals 1 for an ideal gas and departs from 1 for real gases at high reduced pressure
questions.why: Z measures departure from ideal behaviour; it is close to 1 at low reduced pressure or high reduced temperature and departs from 1 at high pressure. Steam near saturation is far from ideal, so tables must be used. Real gases can have Z below 1 (where attractive forces dominate) as well as above 1, so 'always greater than 1' is wrong. In common UK usage a perfect gas has constant specific heats, the opposite of strongly varying ones.

questions.q: A rigid vessel contains 2 kg of water at 1 bar with a total volume of 2 m³. Using v_f ≈ 0.001043 and v_g ≈ 1.694 m³/kg at 1 bar (approximate table values), determine the phase, the dryness fraction and the mass of liquid.
markScheme: v = V/m = 1.0 m³/kg
v_f < v < v_g, so the water is a wet mixture at T_sat ≈ 99.6 °C
Mass of liquid = (1 − x) × 2 ≈ 0.82 kg (vapour ≈ 1.18 kg)
questions.modelAnswer: Specific volume v = V/m = 2/2 = 1.0 m³/kg. At 1 bar, v_f ≈ 0.001043 and v_g ≈ 1.694 m³/kg; since v_f < v < v_g, the contents are a wet liquid–vapour mixture at the saturation temperature, about 99.6 °C. Dryness fraction x = (v − v_f)/(v_g − v_f) = (1.0 − 0.001043)/(1.694 − 0.001043) ≈ 0.59. The vapour mass is about 0.59 × 2 ≈ 1.18 kg, and the liquid mass is about 0.82 kg. Almost all of the volume is occupied by the vapour, even though a substantial mass is liquid.

questions.q: What is the maximum possible thermal efficiency of a heat engine operating between reservoirs at 527 °C and 27 °C?
questions.why: η_Carnot = 1 − T_L/T_H with temperatures in kelvin: 1 − 300/800 = 0.625. 0.949 uses Celsius temperatures (1 − 27/527). 0.375 is T_L/T_H, the fraction of heat rejected, not the efficiency. 0.051 is 27/527, the Celsius ratio, again mixing up efficiency with the heat-rejection fraction.

questions.q: An inventor claims an engine takes 1000 kJ of heat from a source at 900 K, rejects heat to surroundings at 300 K and produces 700 kJ of work per cycle. What can you conclude?
options: The claim violates the First Law
The claim is possible, because 700 kJ is less than 1000 kJ
The claim is possible only if the engine is reversible
The claim violates the Second Law, because the maximum possible work is about 667 kJ
questions.why: The Carnot limit is 1 − 300/900 = 0.667, so at most 667 kJ of work is possible: 700 kJ violates the Second Law. Being less than 1000 kJ only shows the First Law is satisfied (300 kJ is rejected), which is not sufficient. The First Law is not violated, because energy balances. Even a reversible engine reaches only 667 kJ, so reversibility cannot rescue the claim.

questions.q: State the Kelvin–Planck and Clausius statements of the Second Law. A domestic refrigerator keeps its interior at 3 °C in a kitchen at 22 °C. Calculate its maximum possible COP and explain two reasons why a real refrigerator's COP is much lower.
markScheme: Kelvin–Planck: no cyclic device can convert heat from a single reservoir entirely into work
Clausius: no cyclic device can move heat from cold to hot with no other effect (needs work input)
Reason 1: heat transfer across finite temperature differences in evaporator and condenser (so refrigerant runs colder/hotter than the spaces)
Reason 2: irreversibilities such as compressor friction/non-isentropic compression, throttling, pressure drops
questions.modelAnswer: Kelvin–Planck: it is impossible for a device operating in a cycle to receive heat from a single reservoir and produce an equal amount of work, so an engine must reject some heat. Clausius: it is impossible for a cyclic device to transfer heat from a colder body to a hotter one with no other effect, so a refrigerator needs a work input. With T_L = 276.15 K and T_H = 295.15 K, COP_R,max = T_L/(T_H − T_L) = 276.15/19 ≈ 14.5. Real refrigerators achieve far less. First, heat must flow across finite temperature differences: the evaporator runs well below 3 °C and the condenser well above 22 °C, widening the effective temperature lift. Second, the cycle has internal irreversibilities: non-isentropic compression with friction, throttling instead of expansion through a work-producing device, and pressure drops in pipes and heat exchangers.

questions.q: 1000 kJ of heat flows from a reservoir at 500 K to one at 300 K. What is the total entropy generated?
questions.why: S_gen = 1000/300 − 1000/500 = 3.33 − 2.00 = +1.33 kJ/K. Zero would apply only to reversible heat transfer across an infinitesimal temperature difference. −1.33 kJ/K takes the signs the wrong way round and would violate the Second Law. +5.33 kJ/K adds the two magnitudes instead of recognising that the hot reservoir loses entropy.

questions.q: Air at 100 kPa and 300 K is compressed isentropically to 800 kPa (γ = 1.4). What is the outlet temperature?
questions.why: T₂ = T₁(p₂/p₁)^((γ−1)/γ) = 300 × 8^0.2857 ≈ 543 K. 2400 K multiplies by the full pressure ratio, as if T ∝ p (constant volume). 586 K is the actual outlet temperature for a compressor with isentropic efficiency 0.85, not the isentropic value. 689 K uses the exponent γ − 1 = 0.4 instead of (γ − 1)/γ, which is the relation for a volume (compression) ratio, not a pressure ratio.

questions.q: Air (c_p = 1.005 kJ/(kg·K), R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K), γ = 1.4) is compressed adiabatically from 100 kPa, 300 K to 800 kPa in a compressor with isentropic efficiency 0.85. Find the actual outlet temperature, the actual work input per kg and the specific entropy change. Show the process on a T–s sketch.
markScheme: Actual work = c_p(T₂s − T₁)/η = 1.005 × 243.4/0.85 ≈ 287.8 kJ/kg
T–s sketch: vertical line to 2s on the 800 kPa isobar; actual state 2 to the right of 2s on the same isobar; Δs > 0 explained as irreversibility
questions.modelAnswer: Isentropic outlet: T₂s = 300 × (800/100)^(0.4/1.4) = 300 × 8^0.2857 ≈ 543.4 K. Isentropic work = c_p(T₂s − T₁) = 1.005 × 243.4 ≈ 244.7 kJ/kg. The actual work is larger: w = 244.7/0.85 ≈ 287.8 kJ/kg (input). Since w = c_p(T₂ − T₁), T₂ = 300 + 243.4/0.85 ≈ 586.4 K. Entropy change: Δs = c_p ln(T₂/T₁) − R ln(p₂/p₁) = 1.005 ln(586.4/300) − 0.287 ln 8 ≈ 0.6735 − 0.5968 ≈ +0.077 kJ/(kg·K). On a T–s diagram, the ideal process is a vertical line from state 1 up to state 2s on the 800 kPa constant-pressure line. The real state 2 lies on the same pressure line but further right (higher T and s). The entropy increase in an adiabatic process measures the irreversibility (friction and turbulence) in the compressor.

questions.q: What is the ideal Otto cycle efficiency for a compression ratio of 8, with γ = 1.4?
questions.why: η = 1 − 1/r^(γ−1) = 1 − 8^(−0.4) ≈ 0.565. 0.875 is 1 − 1/r, omitting the exponent γ − 1. 0.435 is 8^(−0.4), the fraction of heat rejected, not the efficiency. 0.448 is the Brayton formula with r = 8 treated as a pressure ratio (1 − 8^(−0.2857)).

questions.q: In an ideal Rankine cycle, why is the pump work so much smaller than the turbine work?
options: Because the pump handles a liquid with a very small specific volume, and w ≈ vΔp
Because the pump is more efficient than the turbine
Because the pressure rise across the pump is smaller than the pressure drop across the turbine
Because heat is added in the pump
questions.why: Reversible steady-flow work is −∫v dp, and liquid water's specific volume (about 0.001 m³/kg) is around a thousand times smaller than steam's, so the pump work (about 4 kJ/kg in the example) is tiny. In an ideal cycle both machines are isentropic, so efficiency is not the reason. The pressure rise across the pump equals the pressure drop across the turbine (both work between the same boiler and condenser pressures). No heat is added in the pump; heat is added in the boiler.

questions.q: An ideal vapour-compression refrigerator using R-134a has the following approximate property values: compressor inlet (saturated vapour) h₁ = 239.2 kJ/kg; compressor outlet h₂ = 275.4 kJ/kg; condenser outlet (saturated liquid) h₃ = 95.5 kJ/kg. The mass flow rate is 0.05 kg/s. Find the refrigeration effect, the compressor power and the COP. Explain the role of the throttling valve.
markScheme: Throttle: h₄ = h₃ = 95.5 kJ/kg (adiabatic, no work)
Refrigeration effect Q̇_L = ṁ(h₁ − h₄) = 0.05 × 143.7 ≈ 7.2 kW
Compressor power Ẇ = ṁ(h₂ − h₁) = 0.05 × 36.2 ≈ 1.8 kW
Role of valve: drops pressure (and saturation temperature) so the refrigerant can evaporate below the cold-space temperature; irreversible but simple
questions.modelAnswer: Across the throttling valve there is no work and negligible heat transfer, so h₄ = h₃ = 95.5 kJ/kg. Refrigeration effect: Q̇_L = ṁ(h₁ − h₄) = 0.05 × (239.2 − 95.5) ≈ 7.2 kW. Compressor power: Ẇ = ṁ(h₂ − h₁) = 0.05 × (275.4 − 239.2) ≈ 1.8 kW. COP_R = Q̇_L/Ẇ = 143.7/36.2 ≈ 3.97. The throttling valve drops the refrigerant from condenser to evaporator pressure, lowering its saturation temperature so it can evaporate below the temperature of the cold space and absorb heat. Throttling is irreversible and wastes the work an expansion turbine could recover, but a valve is simple, cheap and reliable, and the work available from expanding a mostly liquid refrigerant is small.

questions.q: A drag force F depends on fluid density ρ, velocity V, diameter D and viscosity μ. According to the Buckingham Π theorem, how many independent dimensionless groups describe the problem?
questions.why: There are n = 5 variables (F, ρ, V, D, μ) and k = 3 base dimensions (M, L, T), giving n − k = 2 groups: F/(ρV²D²) and ρVD/μ. One group would result from forgetting F or μ in the list. Three groups comes from counting only two base dimensions (for example ignoring time). Five is the number of variables, not groups.

questions.q: A 1:4 scale model of a car is tested in a wind tunnel using air at the same conditions as the full-size car, which travels at 25 m/s. For Reynolds number similarity, what model air speed is needed?
questions.why: Re = ρVL/μ must match; with the same fluid, V_m L_m = V_p L_p, so V_m = 25 × 4 = 100 m/s. 6.25 m/s scales the speed down by the model scale instead of up. 25 m/s keeps the speed the same, which would make the model Reynolds number four times too small. 12.5 m/s scales with the square root of the length ratio, which is Froude scaling (V ∝ √L) and gives 25/2 for a smaller model; it is appropriate for free-surface flows, not Reynolds similarity.

questions.q: The period t of a simple pendulum may depend on its length L, the bob mass m and the gravitational acceleration g. Use dimensional analysis to find the form of the relationship, and explain what the result shows about mass. Why can dimensional analysis not give the numerical constant?
markScheme: Dimensions: t [T], L [L], m [M], g [L T⁻²]
n = 4, k = 3 → one Π group
Π = t g^a L^b m^c dimensionless: M: c = 0; T: 1 − 2a = 0 → a = ½; L: a + b = 0 → b = −½
Π = t√(g/L) = constant, so t = C√(L/g)
Mass cannot appear (no other variable contains M); constant (2π for small swings) needs physics/experiment
questions.modelAnswer: List the variables and dimensions: t [T], L [L], m [M], g [L T⁻²]. There are n = 4 variables and k = 3 base dimensions, so there is n − k = 1 dimensionless group, which must therefore equal a constant. Seek Π = t g^a L^b m^c. M: c = 0. T: 1 − 2a = 0, so a = ½. L: a + b = 0, so b = −½. Hence Π = t√(g/L) = C, i.e. t = C√(L/g). Mass drops out because it is the only variable containing M, so nothing could cancel its dimension: the period does not depend on the bob's mass. Dimensional analysis cannot find C, because a pure number has no dimensions. Solving the equation of motion (or experiment) gives C = 2π for small oscillations.

questions.q: In the Reynolds Transport Theorem for a fixed control volume, what does the term ∫_CS ρb(V·n) dA represent?
options: The rate of change of B stored inside the control volume
The total amount of B in the system
The net rate at which B flows out across the control surface
The force acting on the control volume
questions.why: The surface integral is the net outflow rate of the property B across the control surface (positive V·n where fluid leaves). The storage term d/dt ∫_CV ρb dV is the rate of change inside the CV. The total amount of B in the system is B_sys itself, not a rate. Forces enter only when b = V and the left-hand side is replaced by ΣF; the integral itself is a momentum flux, not a force.

questions.q: A tank receives water at 5 kg/s and loses 3 kg/s through an outlet. Its plan area is 0.5 m². At what rate does the water level change?
questions.why: dm/dt = 5 − 3 = 2 kg/s, so dh/dt = 2/(ρA) = 2/(1000 × 0.5) = 0.004 m/s = 4 mm/s, rising. 4 m/s divides by the area but forgets the density. 'Falls' reverses the sign of the net inflow. 16 mm/s uses the sum of the flows (8 kg/s) instead of the difference.

questions.q: Explain the difference between a system and a control volume, and why the Reynolds Transport Theorem is needed in fluid mechanics. Show how setting b = 1 gives the continuity equation for steady flow with one inlet and one outlet.
markScheme: System: fixed identity/mass, moves and deforms with the flow (Lagrangian)
CV: fixed region in space that fluid crosses (Eulerian); convenient for devices and measurements
Basic laws are stated for systems, so RTT converts them to CV form
b = 1: dm_sys/dt = 0 = d/dt ∫ρ dV + ∫ρ V·n dA; steady → ∫ρ V·n dA = 0 → ṁ_out = ṁ_in (ρ₁A₁V₁ = ρ₂A₂V₂)
questions.modelAnswer: A system is a fixed collection of fluid particles that moves and deforms with the flow (a Lagrangian view); its mass is constant by definition. A control volume is a chosen region in space through which fluid passes (an Eulerian view), which suits devices such as pumps and nozzles and how measurements are made. The fundamental laws of mass, momentum and energy are stated for systems, so the Reynolds Transport Theorem is needed to rewrite them for a control volume. With B = m and b = 1: dm_sys/dt = 0 = d/dt ∫_CV ρ dV + ∫_CS ρ(V·n) dA. For steady flow the storage term vanishes, so ∫_CS ρ(V·n) dA = 0. With uniform flow at one inlet and one outlet this gives ρ₂A₂V₂ − ρ₁A₁V₁ = 0, i.e. ṁ_in = ṁ_out.

questions.q: A 50 mm diameter water jet at 20 m/s strikes a fixed flat plate normally and spreads out radially along it. What force does it exert on the plate?
questions.why: F = ṁV = ρAV² = 1000 × (π/4 × 0.05²) × 20² ≈ 785 N, since the jet's momentum in its original direction is reduced to zero. 39.3 N is the mass flow rate (kg/s) mistaken for a force. 393 N uses ½ρAV², treating the problem like a dynamic pressure on the jet area. 1571 N doubles the result, which would apply only if the jet were turned right back on itself (180° deflection by a cup-shaped vane).

questions.q: Which of the following situations allows Bernoulli's equation to be applied directly between two points?
options: Through a long pipe in which friction causes a large pressure drop
Along a streamline in steady flow of water through a smooth, short contraction
Across a sudden pipe expansion with large eddies
questions.why: A short, smooth contraction in steady incompressible flow has negligible losses, so Bernoulli applies along a streamline. A pump adds shaft work, which Bernoulli does not include. A sudden expansion has significant eddy losses (use momentum and the energy equation with h_L). In a long pipe, viscous friction causes a head loss, so the inviscid assumption fails.

questions.q: Water flows at 0.01 m³/s through a horizontal nozzle that reduces from 80 mm to 30 mm diameter and discharges to atmosphere. Neglecting losses and the weight of water, find the gauge pressure at the nozzle inlet and the force needed to hold the nozzle in place, stating its direction.
markScheme: Continuity: V₁ = Q/A₁ ≈ 1.99 m/s, V₂ = Q/A₂ ≈ 14.15 m/s
Bernoulli (horizontal, p₂ = 0 gauge): p₁ = ½ρ(V₂² − V₁²) ≈ 98.1 kPa
Momentum on CV: p₁A₁ + F_x = ṁ(V₂ − V₁), ṁ = 10 kg/s
F_x = 121.6 − 493.1 ≈ −371.5 N on the water (upstream)
Water pushes nozzle downstream with ≈ 371.5 N, so the coupling must restrain it with ≈ 371.5 N acting upstream
questions.modelAnswer: Areas: A₁ = π/4 × 0.08² = 5.027 × 10⁻³ m² and A₂ = π/4 × 0.03² = 7.069 × 10⁻⁴ m². Continuity gives V₁ = 0.01/A₁ ≈ 1.99 m/s and V₂ = 0.01/A₂ ≈ 14.15 m/s. Bernoulli between inlet and outlet (horizontal; outlet at atmospheric pressure, so p₂ = 0 gauge): p₁ = ½ × 1000 × (14.15² − 1.99²) ≈ 98.1 kPa gauge. Momentum in the flow direction for a CV enclosing the water in the nozzle, using gauge pressures: p₁A₁ + F_x = ṁ(V₂ − V₁), where F_x is the force from the nozzle walls on the water and ṁ = 10 kg/s. So F_x = 10 × (14.15 − 1.99) − 98 091 × 5.027 × 10⁻³ ≈ 121.6 − 493.1 ≈ −371.5 N, i.e. the nozzle pushes the water upstream. By Newton's third law the water pushes the nozzle downstream with about 371.5 N, so the coupling or bolts must hold the nozzle with about 371.5 N acting upstream (bolts in tension).

questions.q: Oil (ρ = 900 kg/m³, μ = 0.1 Pa·s) flows at a mean velocity of 1 m/s in a 20 mm diameter pipe. What is the pressure drop over 10 m?
questions.why: Re = 900 × 1 × 0.02/0.1 = 180, so the flow is laminar and Δp = 32μLV/D² = 32 × 0.1 × 10 × 1/0.02² = 80 kPa. 20 kPa uses the Fanning friction factor 16/Re in the Darcy equation Δp = f(L/D)ρV²/2, which expects the Darcy value 64/Re. 320 kPa uses the radius (0.01 m) in place of the diameter in a formula written for D. 1.6 kPa divides by D instead of D² (32 × 0.1 × 10 × 1/0.02 = 1600 Pa), a dimensional slip.

questions.q: In fully developed laminar flow in a circular pipe, how does the centreline velocity compare with the mean velocity?
options: It is about 1.2 times the mean velocity
It is 2 times the mean velocity
It is 1.5 times the mean velocity
questions.why: The profile is parabolic, u = u_max(1 − r²/R²), and integrating over the circular area gives V̄ = u_max/2, so u_max = 2V̄. Equal velocities would mean a flat (plug) profile, which violates no-slip. 1.5 times is the result for laminar flow between parallel plates, not in a pipe. About 1.2 times is typical of a flatter turbulent profile.

questions.q: For the oil flow of the previous question (ρ = 900 kg/m³, μ = 0.1 Pa·s, D = 20 mm, V̄ = 1 m/s, L = 10 m), verify that the flow is laminar, then use the Darcy–Weisbach equation with f = 64/Re to find the head loss and the pressure drop. Find also the wall shear stress and the pumping power needed to overcome friction.
markScheme: Re = 180 < ~2000 → laminar
Δp = ρgh_f ≈ 80 kPa (matches 32μLV/D²)
questions.modelAnswer: Re = ρVD/μ = 900 × 1 × 0.02/0.1 = 180, well below about 2000, so the flow is laminar. f = 64/Re = 64/180 ≈ 0.356. Head loss: h_f = f(L/D)(V²/2g) = 0.356 × (10/0.02) × 1²/(2 × 9.81) ≈ 9.06 m of oil. Pressure drop: Δp = ρgh_f = 900 × 9.81 × 9.06 ≈ 80 kPa, which agrees with Hagen–Poiseuille, Δp = 32μLV/D² = 80 kPa. Wall shear stress from a force balance on the fluid in the pipe: τ_w πDL = Δp πD²/4, so τ_w = ΔpD/(4L) = 80 000 × 0.02/40 = 40 Pa. Flow rate Q = π/4 × 0.02² × 1 ≈ 3.14 × 10⁻⁴ m³/s, so the pumping power to overcome friction is QΔp ≈ 3.14 × 10⁻⁴ × 80 000 ≈ 25 W.

questions.q:
A simple steam power plant operates on an ideal Rankine cycle. Steam leaves the boiler and enters the turbine at 4 MPa and 400 °C, and the condenser pressure is 10 kPa. Use these steam table values (IAPWS-95-based, as in Çengel and Boles, Tables A-5 and A-6): at 4 MPa, 400 °C: h = 3214.5 kJ/kg, s = 6.7714 kJ/(kg·K). At 10 kPa: T_sat = 45.8 °C, v_f = 0.001010 m³/kg, h_f = 191.8 kJ/kg, h_fg = 2392.1 kJ/kg, s_f = 0.6492 kJ/(kg·K), s_fg = 7.4996 kJ/(kg·K).
(a) Sketch the plant and the cycle on a T–s diagram, numbering the states. [4]
(b) Find the dryness fraction and enthalpy at turbine exit. [4]
(c) Find the turbine work, pump work and heat input per kg. [6]
(d) Find the thermal efficiency and compare it with the Carnot efficiency between the same maximum and minimum temperatures. [5]
(e) The real turbine has an isentropic efficiency of 0.85. Find the new turbine exit enthalpy and dryness fraction, and the new cycle efficiency. Comment on the result. [6]
markScheme: (a) Correct plant sketch (boiler, turbine, condenser, pump) and T–s diagram with dome, states 1–4
(d) Explains gap: heat added over a range of temperatures (mean T of heat addition well below 400 °C)
(e) η ≈ (909.4 − 4.0)/3018.7 ≈ 0.300; comment on irreversibility reducing output, drier exhaust
Approximate table values acknowledged; units and signs consistent
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Plant: pump (3→4) feeds compressed liquid to the boiler (4→1), superheated steam expands in the turbine (1→2), and wet steam condenses (2→3) to saturated liquid. On a T–s diagram: 3→4 is a short vertical line (isentropic pumping) just left of the saturated liquid line; 4→1 follows the 4 MPa constant-pressure line through the dome into the superheat region; 1→2 is vertical (isentropic expansion) into the wet region; 2→3 is horizontal at 45.8 °C.

(b) Isentropic expansion: s₂ = s₁ = 6.7714. x₂ = (6.7714 − 0.6492)/7.4996 ≈ 0.8163. h₂ = 191.8 + 0.8163 × 2392.1 ≈ 2144.6 kJ/kg (keep four figures in x: rounding to 0.816 gives 2143.8 kJ/kg).

(c) Turbine work: w_T = h₁ − h₂ = 3214.5 − 2144.6 ≈ 1069.9 kJ/kg. Pump work: w_P = v_f(p₄ − p₃) = 0.00101 × (4000 − 10) ≈ 4.0 kJ/kg (input), so h₄ = 191.8 + 4.0 = 195.8 kJ/kg. Heat input: q_in = h₁ − h₄ = 3214.5 − 195.8 ≈ 3018.7 kJ/kg.

(d) Net work = 1069.9 − 4.0 ≈ 1065.9 kJ/kg, so η = 1065.9/3018.7 ≈ 0.353 (35.3%). Check: q_out = h₂ − h₃ ≈ 1952.8 kJ/kg and q_in − q_out ≈ 1065.9 kJ/kg, consistent. The Carnot efficiency between 400 °C (673.15 K) and 45.8 °C (318.95 K) is 1 − 318.95/673.15 ≈ 0.526. The Rankine efficiency is lower because much of the heat is added at temperatures well below 400 °C (heating the feed water and boiling at about 250 °C), so the mean temperature of heat addition is low.

(e) Actual turbine work = 0.85 × 1069.9 ≈ 909.4 kJ/kg, so h₂' = 3214.5 − 909.4 ≈ 2305.1 kJ/kg and x₂' = (2305.1 − 191.8)/2392.1 ≈ 0.883. Heat input is unchanged (3018.7 kJ/kg), so η = (909.4 − 4.0)/3018.7 ≈ 0.300. Turbine irreversibility cuts efficiency by about 5 percentage points; the lost work appears as extra heat rejected in the condenser. The exhaust is drier (x ≈ 0.88 instead of 0.82), which slightly reduces blade erosion, but this is a by-product, not an advantage. (All values depend on the approximate table data used.)

questions.q:
Lubricating oil (ρ = 880 kg/m³, μ = 0.08 Pa·s) is pumped through a horizontal pipe of diameter 25 mm and length 30 m at a volume flow rate of 0.4 litres per second. The pipe discharges to atmosphere.
(a) Calculate the mean velocity and Reynolds number, and confirm the flow regime. [4]
(b) Starting from a force balance on a cylindrical element of fluid, show that the shear stress varies linearly with radius, and state the velocity profile that results. [5]
(c) Calculate the pressure drop along the pipe and the required gauge pressure at the pump outlet. [4]
(d) Calculate the wall shear stress and the maximum velocity. [3]
(e) Calculate the pumping power and explain how it would change if the pipe diameter were halved for the same flow rate. [4]
markScheme: (b) Force balance: Δp πr² = τ 2πrL → τ = (Δp/L)(r/2), linear in r; with τ = −μ du/dr and no-slip → parabolic u = u_max(1 − r²/R²)
(c) Δp = 32μLV̄/D² ≈ 100 kPa; pump outlet gauge ≈ 100 kPa (exit at atmosphere, KE change negligible/unchanged)
(d) τ_w = ΔpD/(4L) ≈ 20.9 Pa; u_max = 2V̄ ≈ 1.63 m/s
(e) Power = QΔp ≈ 40 W
(e) Halving D at same Q: Δp ∝ 1/D⁴ → ×16, power ×16 ≈ 640 W (Re doubles to ≈ 448, still laminar)
Clear units and assumptions (steady, fully developed, Newtonian, laminar)
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) A = π/4 × 0.025² = 4.909 × 10⁻⁴ m². V̄ = Q/A = 0.0004/4.909 × 10⁻⁴ ≈ 0.815 m/s. Re = ρV̄D/μ = 880 × 0.815 × 0.025/0.08 ≈ 224, well below about 2000, so the flow is laminar.

(b) Take a coaxial cylinder of fluid of radius r and length L. In steady, fully developed flow there is no change in momentum, so the net pressure force balances the shear force on its curved surface: Δp πr² = τ(2πrL), so τ = (Δp/L)(r/2). Shear stress is zero on the axis and rises linearly to τ_w = (Δp/L)(R/2) = ΔpD/(4L) at the wall. With Newton's law of viscosity τ = −μ du/dr: du/dr = −(Δp/(2μL))r, and integrating with u = 0 at r = R (no-slip) gives u = (Δp/(4μL))(R² − r²) = u_max(1 − r²/R²), a parabolic profile.

(c) Integrating the profile gives Δp = 32μLV̄/D² = 32 × 0.08 × 30 × 0.815/0.025² ≈ 1.00 × 10⁵ Pa ≈ 100 kPa. Since the pipe is horizontal, discharges to atmosphere and has constant diameter (no change in kinetic energy), the pump outlet gauge pressure must be about 100 kPa.

(d) τ_w = ΔpD/(4L) = 100 000 × 0.025/120 ≈ 20.9 Pa. u_max = 2V̄ ≈ 1.63 m/s.

(e) Pumping power = QΔp = 0.0004 × 100 000 ≈ 40 W. From Hagen–Poiseuille, Δp = 128μLQ/(πD⁴), so at fixed Q, Δp ∝ 1/D⁴. Halving the diameter multiplies the pressure drop and the power by 16, to about 1.6 MPa and 640 W. The Reynolds number doubles to about 448 (Re ∝ Q/D at fixed Q), so the flow remains laminar and the analysis still holds. This strong D⁴ dependence is why undersized pipes are so costly to pump through.
